title: Voices
intro: Voices is about navigating other people's speech while keeping a voice of one's own. Advice to listen carefully and see the world sits beside gossip, mutual contempt and demands to keep quiet. The speaker is not consistently outside that system: everyone is implicated, and silence can be both self-protection and avoidance. The classroom image makes the problem especially clear. Everybody knows something, but each waits for somebody else to raise it. The return to youthful curiosity at the end preserves another possibility: listen without surrendering your own judgement.
reading: Listening versus silencing; shared complicity makes privacy and avoidance hard to separate.

revisions.editorial-9-own-voice: The advice to remember your own voice comes after encouragement to go out while young and see beautiful things. The song is not simply recommending withdrawal from a corrupt world. It asks for a difficult combination: remain open to experience and other people, but do not let their speech replace your own. Returning to this advice at the end prevents the intervening demand for silence from becoming the song's only answer.
revisions.editorial-9-clean: Saying nobody is clean undermines the easy division between an innocent speaker and malicious outsiders. It challenges people's right to condemn one another, but it can also become a reason not to challenge anything at all. The next movement toward quiet carries that ambiguity. Shared imperfection might encourage humility; shared implication might encourage everyone to protect one another by saying nothing.
revisions.editorial-9-sit-nicely: The command sounds like an adult arranging obedient children. In a song that has just encouraged young people to find their own voice, that change of register is sharp. The speaker wants relief from noise, yet starts using the language of the authority that controls who may speak. This is a tension within the voice of the song, not proof that every command should be read as a separate political code.
revisions.editorial-9-known-secret: Everybody already knows the supposed secret. What is missing is someone willing to make that knowledge public, like a class waiting for another pupil to ask the question. The lyric does not identify the concealed matter, so supplying a particular scandal would narrow it without evidence. Its precise observation is about shared hesitation: a room can be full of knowledge and still behave as though nobody knows.
revisions.9-miracle: The impossible or exceedingly rare events arrive after the collective refusal to speak. Waiting for a miracle lets people postpone the ordinary action that might change the situation. A cycad flowering and the sun rising in the west make that postponement sound absurdly patient. The song's closing advice to preserve one's own voice becomes more pointed after this scene of everyone waiting for somebody else.
